while examining the echolocation calls in graph b, some calls are outside of the range of *myotis daubentonii* in transit according to the graphs that plot the fme/signal duration and the fme/ef.  the calls with a signal duration of 6 ms and an end frequency of 29 khz are outside the range of *m. daubentonii* above water. *m. daubentonii* alongside a forrest edge was out of the question with certain calls in all the graphs. all the calls are within the range of *m. capaccinii* in all the graphs.

remarks: clear echolocation of a serotine bat in flight. fm-qcf calls with a peak frequency around 25 khz.

the calls in this recording are from serotine bats that were emerging from the maternity roost where at least 30 individuals reside. at first i thought we were recording echolocation of long-eared bats, but it was clear from the video footage (and the time of emerging) that these were serotine bats. the specifications of the calls do not match with the specifications given in the book "bat calls of britain and europe" by jon russ. the minimum / end frequency of the calls are around 31 khz and the peak frequency of the calls are around 35 khz.

these recordings made me really excited, because i finally recorded the w-type social calls of the nathusius' pipistrelle as described by helena jahelková (2011)! a little later, two bats were present and one bat emitted the more typical type d social calls. however, part d motifs - associated with advertising bats - was also present.

a citing from her paper: "in may and june, a continuous social vocalization of quite unusual structure and composition was recorded apart from these standard calls. most of these calls were designed in a long “wavy line” pattern with the peak frequency of 14–36 khz, and were accompanied by standard or modified echolocation calls. in one case we succeeded to supplement the acoustic records with a complete record of behavioural details: two bats slowly flew and followed one another in a circular path in front of the roost, where they repeatedly performed false landings, and during approaching one of them emitted the unusual social calls."

- helena jahelková (2011). unusual social calls of nathusius' pipistrelle (vespertilionidae, chiroptera) recorded outside the mating season. institute of vertebrate biology, czech academy of sciences. folia zoologica, 60(1): 25-30. https://doi.org/10.25225/fozo.v60.i1.a4.2011

remarks:
sometimes identifying calls are like solving a mystery game. the following recording contains calls between 20 - 30 khz. at first i thought of a plecotus, but the peak frequency is quite low and no harmonics are present. could it be social calls of the common pipistrelles? they do share a lot of similarity with the recording of type c social calls from a common pipistrelle of c. parnwell, thought to relate to a juvenile in tandem flight (neil middleton et al., 2020). three common pipistrelles are present within the recodring. the loudest being the pipistrelle with the peak frequency around 46,5 khz (bat a), the second loudest being the pipistrelle with the peak frequency around 42,5 khz (bat b) and the third being the most in the distance with the peak frequency around 43,5 khz (bat c). in the first and the third snippit, an echolocation call of bat c is right above a mystery call, disqualifying this bat as the one emitting the lower-frequency calls. in third snippit, bat a is right above a mystery call, also excluding this bat from the options and leaving bat b as the only plausibility.

then i noticed bat b having a few echolocation calls with the peak frequency around 40,7 khz. bat b is a nathusius' pipistrelle. these calls are part b of their general type d social call.

- neil middleton, andrew froud and keith french (2022). social calls of the bats of britain and ireland (second edition). pelagic publishing. page 182.

the similarity of these social calls to the xc upload xc911809 and xc911810 makes me assume that these calls might be from nathusius' pipistrelle from within the roost as well. no indications for a roost, such as bats entering the building or tapping a possible roost entrance, were seen. it is a possibility that the roost entrance was on the side of the building that was out of sight.

- jon russ (2021). bat calls of britain and europe: a guide to species identification. pelagic publishing.

remarks: type c and type d social calls of the common noctule. recorded not far away from their roost.

two of our fieldworkers found a roost of the common noctule in a tree, assumed to be a mating roost. one bat was clearly visible sitting inside the tree hole, while it was emitting calls. this bat is assumed to be the male. the calls are very similar to the recordings of jon russ of a male noctule calling from a tree (russ, 2021). a few encounters with a close-approaching bat, assumed to be female, took place. a big variety of social calls were recorded.

- jon russ (2021). bat calls of britain and europe: a guide to species identification. pelagic publishing.

snr-quality: e (12 db iso / itu)

read all about snr-quality assesment [here](https://xeno-canto.org/article/275).

this recording is a "bycatch" of an automatic recording of the morning communication of hooded crows (corvus cornix). i assume that the bat/s was/were returning from its/their nightly hunt/s to its/their hideout/s. i noticed the signals by coincidence when i was checking the sonograms in audacity. in the beginning there is a sound which is unusually low in frequnecy for a bat, so this may be a mechanical or machinery sound. 

urban backyard with bushes and small trees.
